notes.meaning: Jehoahaz son of Jehu began his seventeen-year rule over the northern kingdom of Israel while Joash was king over Judah. His rise to the throne carried out God's promise that Jehu's family would rule for four generations. Even when Israel was morally weak, God remained faithful to His word.

Jehoahaz continued the false worship begun by Jeroboam, who had set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan to stop people from traveling to worship in Jerusalem. Instead of trusting the Lord, the king held on to this counterfeit religion for political security. Following the sinful patterns of earlier generations leads an entire nation into deeper trouble.

God allowed Hazael and his son Ben-hadad of Aram to overpower Israel because of their persistent disobedience. Without God's defense, Israel was left helpless before a cruel foreign invader. God often allows painful consequences to awaken His people to their need for Him.

Under the crushing weight of Syrian cruelty, King Jehoahaz finally begged God for help, and the Lord listened to him. God responded not because Jehoahaz had lived a righteous life, but because He took pity on His suffering people. Even when our own choices cause our distress, God remains merciful when we cry out to Him.

God provided a deliverer who broke the Syrian hold, allowing the Israelites to live in safety in their homes once again. Commentators traditionally identify this deliverer as the military victories God granted through Jehoahaz's son Joash and grandson Jeroboam II. God can send rescue and restore peace even to an undeserving people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars identify the deliverer as King Adad-Nirari III of Assyria, whose military attack on Damascus pulled Syrian forces away from Israel.

notes.meaning: Even after experiencing God's deliverance, the people refused to abandon Jeroboam's sins, and an Asherah pole—a wooden idol used to worship a false goddess—remained in Samaria. They wanted relief from their suffering, but they did not want to turn away from their idols. True repentance means giving up the sin itself, not just wanting to escape its pain.

The Syrian army devastated Israel's military so completely that Jehoahaz was left with only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand soldiers. The Aramean king crushed them like chaff scattered and blown away on a threshing floor. When a nation forsakes God, even its greatest earthly defenses can vanish quickly.

The writer closes the record of Jehoahaz by noting that his other accomplishments were preserved in the royal records of Israel. When he died, he was buried in Samaria, and his son Jehoash took the throne. Personal bravery and political titles cannot make up for a lifetime spent walking away from God.

Jehoash began his sixteen-year rule over Israel during the thirty-seventh year of King Joash of Judah. For the first few years, he likely shared the throne with his father before ruling on his own. God continued to keep His promise to preserve the royal line of Jehu.

Like his father, Jehoash did evil in God's eyes by continuing the golden calf worship started by Jeroboam. Even though this religion had become a long-standing national tradition, God judged it as wicked rebellion. Long-standing custom never makes wrong worship right before God.

The official summary of Jehoash points to his military power, especially his war against King Amaziah of Judah. When he died, he was buried among Israel's kings in Samaria, and his son Jeroboam II followed him on the throne. Human history records earthly conquests, but God remembers whether a person obeyed Him.

Elisha became sick with the illness that would end his life, and King Jehoash came to visit him and wept over him. The king called him the chariots and horsemen of Israel, realizing the prophet's prayers and counsel had protected the country far better than any army. Faithful servants of God are often the greatest shield a nation has.

Elisha instructed the king to take a bow and arrows, and the king obeyed. The prophet used these ordinary weapons of war to stage an acted-out prophecy of coming battles. God often uses familiar everyday things to give spiritual instruction.

Elisha told the king to hold the bow, and then the dying prophet laid his own hands over the king's hands. This symbolic action showed that the strength to win would come from the Lord, not from the king's military power alone. Our work succeeds only when God's power guides and strengthens our hands.

The king opened the window facing east toward the territory stolen by Aram, and Elisha commanded him to shoot. The prophet announced that the arrow represented the Lord's victory, promising that Israel would shatter Aram at the border city of Aphek. When God gives a promise of deliverance, we are invited to act boldly on His word.

Elisha next told the king to take the arrows and strike the ground, testing the depth of the king's faith and zeal. Jehoash struck the ground only three times and then stopped. A casual or half-hearted attitude can keep us from receiving everything God is willing to do.

Elisha was angry that the king had stopped, telling him he should have struck five or six times so that Aram would have been completely wiped out. Because the king lacked bold faith and perseverance, he was told Israel would defeat Aram only three times. A weak faith often limits the blessing God desires to grant.

differ.view: The king's lack of zeal and faith was his own failure, and his half-hearted effort directly limited the victories God gave him.

notes.meaning: Elisha died and was laid in a tomb, and every spring Moabite raiding bands began invading Israelite territory. The death of a faithful prophet who had guarded the nation in prayer left Israel exposed to fresh troubles. Losing godly leaders who intercede for others brings real danger to a land.

While some Israelites were burying a man, they saw raiders approaching and quickly tossed the body into Elisha's open tomb. The moment the body touched Elisha's bones, the dead man came back to life and stood on his feet. God worked this unique miracle to show that His life-giving power outlasts death and that the promises spoken through Elisha were absolutely trustworthy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some interpreters suggest the man was not truly dead but only unconscious, and the shock of the fall or the cold cave woke him up.

notes.meaning: Hazael king of Aram had kept Israel under heavy oppression throughout the entire reign of Jehoahaz. This long suffering was the exact discipline God had warned would come upon them for their worship of idols. God lets His people feel the painful cost of walking away from His protection.

Despite Israel's repeated unfaithfulness, the Lord showed them great mercy and refused to destroy them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. His deep compassion spared them from total destruction at that time. God's kindness to His people flows from His own unchanging promises, not from their goodness.

Hazael died, and his son Ben-hadad became king over Aram in his place. The passing of this fierce enemy opened the way for Israel's recovery just as Elisha had prophesied. Earthly oppressors will always pass away, but God's promises remain firm.

Jehoash defeated Ben-hadad three times in battle and won back all the Israelite cities Hazael had stolen from his father. This three-fold victory matched the exact number of times the king had struck the ground with the arrows before the dying prophet. God fulfilled His word completely, giving the exact measure of victory He had promised.
